findings.where: Article specimen: the subheads 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' and 'Download', at both widths
findings.fault: The subheads are set in a heavy, wide black grotesque. That makes a third typeface, which is neither Newsreader nor Public Sans. The tile's own type-pair note says subheads are Newsreader 500. Between the fine serif title and the serif body, these heads are the loudest and most mechanical text in the article. They read like a tech blog's headings, not like a legal journal's.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder. The brief asks for serious, refined type and 'nothing in-your-face techy', and this is the page Angélique will fill most often, so the clash would repeat on every article. A development-bank reader who meets a slab-heavy sans in the middle of a quiet serif essay sees a break in voice that undercuts the 'editorial gravitas' the direction promises.

findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', compared with the hero line 'In my view, we are at a turning point…'
findings.fault: The site's two largest serif lines use opposite weights. The homepage line is a light, high-contrast display cut. The article title is a heavy bold of the same family, set tight. The type pair gives no bold display weight (300 for the line, 400 for reading, 500 for subheads), so the article page doesn't sound like the same paper as the homepage. The heavy title also crowds its own byline.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges whether the tile holds together as one identity. A visitor going from the home page to an article meets a different, heavier voice, and the 'large light serif' carried over from Freshfields is lost on the page that holds the product.

findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best…'
findings.fault: The title uses a straight typewriter apostrophe in 'World's', while the body text around it uses curly quotes and apostrophes (‘chapter topics’, “What is the best…”). At display size the straight mark is very obvious.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, and Mark as a lawyer used to well-set documents. A dumb quote at headline size is a typesetting slip that cheapens the 'well-set brief' impression this direction is selling.
